entries.title: Tamazight at a glance
body: Tamazight is the name for the Amazigh (Berber) languages of North Africa, a branch of the Afroasiatic family. In Morocco, where the three main varieties are Tarifit in the north, Central Atlas Tamazight in the middle and Tashelhit in the south, about a quarter to a third of people speak one of them.

Standard Moroccan Tamazight was developed by the Royal Institute of Amazigh Culture (IRCAM) from these varieties. It became an official language of Morocco in 2011, next to Arabic, and is taught in schools in Tifinagh.

entries.title: Tifinagh
body: Tifinagh descends from the ancient Libyco-Berber script, which was kept alive by the Tuareg. The modern Neo-Tifinagh alphabet used in Morocco has 33 letters, written left to right with spaces between words.

Every vowel is written, and there are only three full vowels plus a short e sound (ⴻ in some spellings). Letters are mostly circles, lines, dots and crosses. The letter ⵣ, yaz, is the symbol of the Amazigh people and appears on their flag.

entries.title: Gender and number
entries.body: Feminine nouns are wrapped in ⵜ…ⵜ. Regular plurals change the first vowel to ⵉ and add ⵏ (masculine) or ⵉⵏ (feminine). The table shows “student” and “teacher”.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.body: Amazigh numbers are used for one to ten; for larger numbers and prices, many speakers use Arabic numbers.

examples.e: What is your name? (to a man)

entries.title: Yennayer
body: Yennayer is the Amazigh new year, celebrated around 13 January across North Africa with family meals, often a couscous or a dish with seven vegetables. The Amazigh calendar counts its years from 950 BC, so 2026 is around 2976.
Morocco made Yennayer a national public holiday in 2023, and Algeria did so in 2018.
